Arrive
ar-RYVE
v.i. (to come to a place, especially by water)
Late Latin arripare, to come to shore, from ad ripam, to the bank. The original sense is nautical, and the Authorized Version keeps it: both occurrences are landings after a voyage.

Biblical Definition

Luke, who wrote both passages, uses the word with a sailor's precision. After the storm on the lake, “they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is over against Galilee” (Luke 8:26) — and the landing party met the man with the legion. In the travel diary of the third missionary journey the word marks one port among several: “And we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus” (Acts 20:15). The plainness is the point. Luke was there, he kept the log, and the gospel moved across the Aegean in named stages on ordinary ships. Scripture's arrivals are not vague; they are dated, they are located, and they can be checked. The faith rests on events that happened at particular harbours on particular days.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines arrive as to come to; to reach; to come to or reach by water or by travelling; and hence, to gain or compass by effort.

expand to see more

ARRIVE, v.i. To come to; to reach in progress by water, originally; now used also of coming by land.

ARRIVE, v.i. To reach a point by progressive motion; to gain or compass by effort, practice or study.

ARRIVE, v.i. To happen or occur; as, the event arrived at the expected time.

VOYAGE, n. A passing by sea or water from one place, port or country to another.

HARBOR, n. A port or haven for ships; a lodging for the night; a place of safety.

Key Scripture

Luke 8:26 — "And they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes, which is over against Galilee."

Acts 20:15 — "And we sailed thence, and came the next day over against Chios; and the next day we arrived at Samos, and tarried at Trogyllium; and the next day we came to Miletus."

Luke 8:27 — "And when he went forth to land, there met him out of the city a certain man, which had devils long time, and ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs."

Acts 20:16 — "For Paul had determined to sail by Ephesus, because he would not spend the time in Asia: for he hasted, if it were possible for him, to be at Jerusalem the day of Pentecost."

Modern Corruption

The gospel narratives are often treated as timeless religious stories whose geography is decorative; Luke wrote them as a traveller with a log, naming ports a reader could visit.

expand to see more

A persistent way of handling the gospels and Acts is to treat their value as symbolic and their detail as ornament: what matters is the meaning, and the ports, provinces and dates are local colour. Acts 20:15 is a hard verse for that approach. Chios, Samos, Trogyllium, Miletus, each with the interval between them noted, written by a man using the word we. No one inventing a religion writes a sailing itinerary. The Christian faith is not a set of timeless truths illustrated by stories; it is the report of things that happened, and the report keeps a log.

Luke 8:26 shows what the precision is for. They arrived at a real country, over against Galilee, and there they met a man whose name was Legion. The demoniac, the swine, the terrified townsfolk asking Jesus to depart, and the healed man sent home to publish what great things God had done — all of it happens at a landing place. The recovery is a robust historical confidence: our Lord's power over devils was exercised at an address, on a day, in front of witnesses who counted the pigs.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek katapleo (G2668), to sail down to land; paraballo (G3846), to arrive alongside; ploos (G4144), a voyage; limen (G3040), a harbour.

expand to see more

Greek katapleo (G2668) — to sail down, to put in to shore; they arrived at the country of the Gadarenes.

Greek paraballo (G3846) — to throw alongside, to arrive at; we arrived at Samos.

Greek ploos (G4144) — a voyage, a sailing; the setting of Luke's we-passages.

Greek limen (G3040) — a harbour; the named ports of Acts 20 and 27.

Greek legion (G3003) — a legion; the name given at the landing in Luke 8.

Usage

"“They arrived at the country of the Gadarenes” — a real shore."

"“The next day we arrived at Samos” — a log, not a legend."

"“And tarried at Trogyllium” — detail no myth-maker supplies."
